teaser: He was the 75th man to rule Venice. Bellini painted him like a marble bust that breathes.
review_notes:
Loredan as 75th doge, born 1436, elected 2 October 1501, died 1521.
Portrait usually dated 1501 to 1502; oil on poplar, 61.4 x 44.5 cm (National Gallery gives 61.4 x 44.5).
Rough paint used to imitate gold thread in the damask (National Gallery technical notes).
Reading of the two halves of the face (sterner lit side, gentler shadowed side) is a common National Gallery interpretation, not a documented intention.
Dürer's 1506 letter from Venice calling Bellini very old and still the best in painting (paraphrased).
Bought by the National Gallery in 1844; earlier owned by William Beckford.
Antonello da Messina in Venice 1475 to 1476 as a spur to oil painting there.

lesson.text: Seventy-five. By the usual count, that is this man's number in a line of rulers going back some eight hundred years. Leonardo Loredan was elected doge, the head of the Venetian Republic, in October 1501. He was 65, and he would hold the office until his death twenty years later.

A doge was not a king. He was chosen by other nobles, watched by councils, and forbidden to pass the job to his sons. What he had was the costume. So Giovanni Bellini, official painter to the Republic, had to show two things at once: a state that never dies and one aging man inside its clothes.

lesson.title: The office
lesson.text: Start with what any doge would have worn.

spots.title: The horned cap
spots.text: This stiff hat with a bump at the back is the corno, worn only by the doge. Under it sits a fine white linen cap whose thin strings hang down past his jaw.

spots.title: The buttons
spots.text: Big ornamental buttons shaped like little bells or nuts run down the front of the mantle. Each one catches a point of light on its upper left.

spots.title: Silk damask
spots.text: Damask is cloth with a pattern woven into it. For the gold threads Bellini left the paint slightly rough, so that it catches real light the way metal thread would.

lesson.text: He is cut off at the chest by a stone ledge, with no hands and no room around him. That is the shape of an ancient Roman bust, the carved head and shoulders that honored great citizens. Venice liked to think of itself as a new Rome, and here its leader sits like a sculpture on a shelf.
Bellini was already an old man in 1501. Five years later the German artist Albrecht Dürer visited Venice and wrote home that Bellini was very old and still the best painter in the city.

But marble does not have skin. Bellini worked in oil paint, a slow-drying medium that Venetian painters had taken up in his lifetime. It let him lay thin, see-through layers one over another, so that light seems to sink into the cheek and come back out. Now compare the two halves of that face.

lesson.title: The man
lesson.text: The light comes from the left. It splits the face in two.

spots.title: The lit side
spots.text: In full light this half is all bone and discipline: the hollow cheek, the hard line running down from the nose, the corner of the mouth held flat.

spots.title: The shadowed side
spots.text: In the soft shade the mouth seems to lift a little and the face warms. Many viewers feel one side judges and the other is kind.

spots.title: The eyes
spots.text: Pale and alert, they look past you to the left. A tiny white spark sits in each. He never meets your gaze, which keeps him out of reach.

lesson.text: Bellini's trick is to make the costume permanent and the face temporary. The robe and cap belong to all doges. The tired, watchful eyes belong to one man in his sixties.

The blue behind him helps. It is not flat: it deepens toward the top like a sky in late afternoon. Earlier portraits often put the sitter against black. Here there is air, and the warm skin and cool blue make each other stronger. One more thing sits in front of all that air, at the very bottom.
Bellini put his name on this picture, and painted it as if it were a real object. Where is it?

spots.title: The paper label
spots.text: A small creased slip of paper seems stuck to the stone ledge. On it, in Latin capitals: IOANNES BELLINVS. Painted labels like this are called cartellini.

lesson.text: Loredan needed the calm look. In 1509 nearly all the great powers of Europe joined forces against Venice, and the Republic lost almost its whole mainland territory in a single battle. It survived, and so did he.
The picture is painted on a board of poplar, the everyday wood of Italian panel painters. Canvas was only starting to take over in Venice, where damp sea air was hard on both walls and wood.

The panel is small, about 61 by 45 centimeters (24 by 18 inches), close to the size of a real head and shoulders. It left Venice at some point, passed through English private hands, and was bought by the National Gallery in London in 1844.

quiz.question: What was a doge?
options: The elected head of the Venetian Republic
quiz.explanation: Doges were elected by fellow nobles and could not pass the office to their sons.

quiz.question: Which ancient art form does the portrait's format imitate?
quiz.explanation: He is cut at the chest above a stone ledge, like a carved Roman bust.

quiz.question: How do the two halves of Loredan's face differ?
options: The lit side looks stern, the shadowed side gentler
quiz.explanation: The light from the left divides the face into a severe half and a softer half.

quiz.question: How did Bellini sign the painting?
options: On a painted slip of paper on the ledge
On the back of the panel only
In the pattern of the damask
quiz.explanation: A fictive paper label, a cartellino, carries IOANNES BELLINVS.

quiz.question: What did oil paint allow Bellini to do?
options: Build thin transparent layers that make skin glow
quiz.explanation: Slow-drying oil can be layered in see-through films.

facts.text: Loredan looks directly into the viewer's eyes.
facts.explanation: His pale eyes look past the viewer to the left.

facts.text: The doge's horned cap is called a corno.
facts.explanation: It was worn only by the doge, over a white linen cap.

facts.text: Loredan ruled Venice for only a few months.
facts.explanation: He was elected in 1501 and held the office for twenty years.
